clue.text: Plays on the green or the pitch

definitions.text: Plays on the green or the pitch

parts.words: Plays on the green or the pitch
parts.note: the clue reads first as someone playing a game on a lawn, then as a cricketer delivering the ball down the pitch; one word covers both the lawn game and the delivery

explanation.surface: Someone spends the afternoon at sport, either on a lawn or on a cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: The word serves as a noun (the lawn game played on a bowling green) and as a verb (what a cricketer does when delivering the ball on the pitch). The pitch is the strip of turf in the middle of a cricket field.
explanation.definitionFit: The lawn game played on a green shares its name with the cricket verb for delivering the ball.

clue.text: Whence 'the habitues fly clean away?

parts.note: regular visitors who are sparrows and the like: they wash in the garden basin and then take wing, clean

explanation.surface: A question about where regular customers leave from, freshly scrubbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habitues' suggests regulars at a club; they are garden birds, and 'fly clean away' means literally fly off clean after washing.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden basin of water where birds wash and splash before flying off.

clue.text: Isle Man

definitions.meaning: an island off the south coast of England, in the English Channel
an archaic word for a person or creature

explanation.surface: A mention of the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as the Isle of Man, but it is two separate definitions. The Isle of Wight is an island off Hampshire in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Wight lies off southern England; 'wight' is also an old word for a human being.

clue.text: A beringed one's week-end

parts.note: the planet wearing rings gives its name to the last day of the week

explanation.surface: A bejewelled person's days off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beringed' suggests someone wearing many rings; it is the ringed planet Saturn, whose day ends the week.
explanation.definitionFit: The day is named after the ringed planet Saturn and falls at the end of the week.

clue.text: Understanding of pith ?

definitions.meaning: read as under-standing, that which stands beneath, which is the Latin root sense of the word
pith is the essential core or real content of something

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a grasp of what matters most in an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Understanding' is not comprehension here: split as 'under' + 'standing' it renders the Latin substantia, 'what stands beneath'. 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the essential matter beneath appearances and the core of an argument are called this; the Latin origin means standing under.

clue.text: Fobbed-off performer?

parts.note: a stamp hanging from a watch chain, and also the circus animal that balances a ball

explanation.surface: An entertainer brushed off with excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fobbed-off' suggests deceived; read literally, it is something hanging off a watch fob, as a signet stamp did. The same word is the circus animal performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A signet stamp hung from a watch fob; the marine mammal performs tricks in circuses.

clue.text: It comprises the rest of the house

definitions.text: It comprises the rest of the house

parts.words: It comprises the rest of the house
parts.note: rest means sleep, not the remainder: the room in a house kept for sleeping

explanation.surface: A description of everything else in a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the rest of the house' seems to mean all the other rooms; 'rest' is sleep, so it is the room for sleeping.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a bedroom, the room in a house where one sleeps.

clue.text: A New Testament story concerns it, as you see

definitions.text: A New Testament story concerns it, as you see

parts.words: A New Testament story concerns it, as you see
parts.note: the parable of the coins entrusted to servants, a coin whose name also means a gift or skill on show

explanation.surface: Someone points out a Bible story that deals with what is in front of you.
explanation.walkthrough: In the parable in Matthew 25, servants are given sums of money in this old unit; the word now means a natural gift, which you can 'see' in action.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient unit of money in the Bible parable, and the source of the modern word for natural ability.

clue.text: What makes a goat so capitally aggressive ?

definitions.text: What makes a goat so capitally aggressive ?

parts.words: What makes a goat so capitally aggressive ?
parts.note: capitally means with the head: the slang word for head joined to the goat's attack of ramming with it

explanation.surface: A question about why goats are such fine fighters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capitally' means excellently, and also with the head (Latin caput). A goat butts with its nut, slang for head; the answer is a spread made from peanuts.
explanation.definitionFit: A spread of ground nuts, read here as a creature that rams with its head.

clue.text: Authoress gets the morning sun her side of the house

parts.note: the sun rises in the east, abbreviated E
a wing is a side section of a house

explanation.surface: A woman writer has a room that catches the early sunlight.
explanation.walkthrough: Juliana Horatia Ewing was a Victorian children's writer. 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Juliana Horatia Ewing was a Victorian writer of children's stories such as Jackanapes.

clue.text: Unerring manipulator ?

parts.note: the clue is a playful description of a body part: unerring suggests correct, and a manipulator is something that handles things

explanation.surface: A description of someone who never fails to pull the strings.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'manipulator' sounds like a schemer, but here it is the hand that manipulates; 'unerring' gives the sense of correct, as in getting it right.
explanation.definitionFit: Most people do their skilled handling with the dominant hand on the correct side, the one never wrong.

clue.text: Thin wood I make into heavy stick

parts.note: a lath is a thin strip of wood

explanation.surface: A carpenter turns a slim strip of timber into a cudgel.
explanation.walkthrough: A LATHI is the long iron-bound bamboo stick carried by police in South Asia. 'make into' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The lathi is a long bamboo club used in India as a weapon.

clue.text: Good fishing when the Tiber's choppy ?

definitions.text: Good fishing when the Tiber's choppy ?

indicators.note: choppy water is broken up, so the letters of the river's name are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the Roman river's name with its possessive S, all six letters used

explanation.surface: An angler on the Roman river hopes for rough water to bring the fish on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'choppy' rearranges TIBERS; the whole clue also says that when fish are biting the fishing is good. Here the possessive S does supply a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish that take the bait are said to be biting, so many of them make good fishing.

clue.text: Shall not get an antelope to turn silky

definitions.note: an adjective standing for a noun, a silk fabric

parts.note: shall not contracts to shan't

indicators.note: to turn here means the antelope's name is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a gnu is an African antelope

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to let an antelope become smooth and glossy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' reverses GNU to UNG. SHANTUNG is a Chinese silk fabric; the adjective 'silky' stands loosely for the cloth. 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Shantung is a coarse, slubbed silk cloth first woven in a Chinese province.

clue.text: It would have been beneath a lady to ride so

definitions.text: It would have been beneath a lady to ride so

parts.words: It would have been beneath a lady to ride so
parts.note: beneath reads as unworthy, but literally the saddle sat under a lady who rode with both legs on one side

explanation.surface: Riding in a certain style would have been unbecoming to a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beneath a lady' seems to mean unworthy of her; in fact the special saddle was literally beneath her, and genteel women rode this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Women once rode with both legs on one side of the horse, on a saddle designed for it.

clue.text: An unshakable grounding in Latin

parts.note: reads as a solid education in the classics, but means the Latin words for firm, solid earth

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster praises a pupil's thorough knowledge of the classical language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounding' looks like basic schooling; it is literal ground, and 'in Latin' says the answer is the Latin phrase for steady land.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means firm land, solid earth that does not shake, as opposed to the sea.

clue.text: Fit up Shakespeare's playhouse to hire to Verdi for this ?.

parts.note: to rig is to fit out or equip
Henry V's prologue calls the theatre 'this wooden O'
to let is to hire out

explanation.surface: A theatre manager equips the Globe to rent it out to an Italian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'wooden O' of Henry V's prologue is the round Elizabethan theatre. The first 'to' is a link; the definition asks which Verdi opera this is.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigoletto is Verdi's opera about a hunchbacked court jester.

clue.text: Young people's state

parts.note: Young is Brigham Young, who led the Mormons west; his people settled an American state

explanation.surface: A remark about the condition young people are in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young' is not youth but Brigham Young, the Mormon leader who brought his followers to Salt Lake City; 'state' is a US state, not a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young founded Salt Lake City in this American state.

clue.text: Waltzer gets lost?

parts.note: a dancer who pauses mid-step, as in the hesitation waltz, seems to have lost the way

explanation.surface: A dancer loses track at the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The hesitation waltz is a dance with deliberate pauses, so a waltzer who stops mid-step looks like one who has lost the thread.
explanation.definitionFit: To pause in uncertainty, as a dancer stalls in the hesitation waltz.

clue.text: Underlines the forces

definitions.meaning: in physics and engineering, the loads and pressures acting on a body

explanation.surface: A reporter emphasises the role of the armed services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the forces' looks like the armed services; it is the physical loads acting on a structure.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphasis given in speech, and the loads borne by materials in engineering, share the same word.

clue.text: Starter's pudding?

parts.note: a race starter's last word is go, and with the contracted let's before it the call runs together into the name of a pudding

explanation.surface: A diner asks what dessert comes with the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' is not a first course but the race starter, whose call ends "(Let)'s go!"; run together as S'GO it is the name of a milk pudding made from palm starch.
explanation.definitionFit: A milk pudding made with starch granules from a palm, a staple British school dessert.

clue.text: Securities current in Suffolk and in Yorks in a back street

parts.note: the Deben is a river flowing through Suffolk

indicators.note: in places the Yorkshire river inside the reversed abbreviation for street
back means the abbreviation for street is written in reverse

parts.note: another current, this time in Yorkshire: the river Ure

explanation.surface: A financier finds bonds circulating in two English counties and in a back alley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns ST into TS, and 'in' puts URE inside it for TURES. The Deben (Suffolk) and the Ure (Yorkshire) are English rivers; 'current' serves both.
explanation.definitionFit: Debentures are bonds issued by a company, secured on its assets and paying fixed interest.

clue.text: Of chanting in church or iconic rites

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A description of singing in a church or at sacred ceremonies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into 'church or iconic rites', where the letters run across chURCH OR IConic.
explanation.definitionFit: Choric describes things relating to a chorus, as in choral chanting.

clue.text: Spring cure for migraine ?

definitions.meaning: the source where water rises from the ground
read as two words, a head that is well again after a migraine

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a seasonal remedy for headaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like a season, but it is a water source; the second reading splits the word into WELL HEAD, a head made healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: The source of a spring where water emerges is its head; a healthy head is the result of a migraine cure.

clue.text: Virginia Woolf's. main work

parts.note: the title of a Woolf novel, read also as the action of the sea, the main

explanation.surface: A question about Virginia Woolf's principal novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' seems to mean chief; it is the sea, whose work is breakers. The Waves (1931) is a Woolf novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Waves is a 1931 novel by Woolf; the sea's motion produces breakers.

clue.text: Welsh part of Asia

definitions.meaning: as a verb, to welsh is to run off without paying a debt

explanation.surface: A geography question about where the Welsh belong in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh' is not about Wales: it is the verb meaning to dodge paying a bet, and the British slang verb 'levant' means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond leaving debts unpaid is an old British slang verb with that spelling; the region is the eastern Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: He rode on 'air, oddly enough, on a dolphin'

definitions.text: He rode on 'air, oddly enough, on a dolphin'

indicators.note: oddly suggests a strange arrangement, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A legendary figure travelled through the air, strangely, on a dolphin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges ON AIR. Arion was the Greek poet who, thrown overboard, was carried to safety on a dolphin's back.
explanation.definitionFit: Arion, the poet of Greek legend, was rescued at sea by a dolphin.

clue.text: He's loopy

parts.note: a man's name which is also a coil or loop of yarn

explanation.surface: Someone is described as crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loopy' seems to mean mad; a hank is a looped coil of yarn, and Hank is also a man's name, so 'He'.
explanation.definitionFit: A coil of wool or rope wound in loops, and also a man's name.

clue.text: Floating or not, his paper mark is valued

definitions.text: Floating or not, his paper mark is valued

parts.words: Floating or not, his paper mark is valued
parts.note: a person casting a ballot, whether undecided or loyal, makes a cross on the paper and that cross counts

explanation.surface: An observation about currency: whether it floats or not, the paper mark has value.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the German paper mark and floating exchange rates; in fact 'floating' describes an undecided elector and the 'paper mark' is the cross on a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who casts a ballot makes a cross on the paper; a floating one is undecided between parties.

clue.text: Very reverend gentleman accused of speeding? He's booked

definitions.text: Very reverend gentleman accused of speeding? He's booked

parts.words: Very reverend gentleman accused of speeding? He's booked
parts.note: a cathedral clergyman called fast by name, and booked both as charged by police and as an author of books

explanation.surface: A senior clergyman is charged with driving too fast and booked by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: A dean is addressed as 'Very Reverend'; 'speeding' suggests a name meaning fast. 'booked' means charged and also in books: Jonathan Swift, Dean of St Patrick's, Dublin, wrote Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift, satirist and author of Gulliver's Travels, was Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin.

clue.text: Test for measles?

parts.note: a random inspection, read literally as examining a patient for the rash of dots that measles brings

explanation.surface: A doctor screens a child for a childhood illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for a random inspection is taken literally: checking someone for the red marks of measles.
explanation.definitionFit: A random inspection without warning, here pictured as examining skin for a rash.

clue.text: Our heat source is back in the cavity

indicators.note: back means the combined letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: the sun is what heats our planet

explanation.surface: Someone explains that warmth is returning to a hollow place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses SUNIS to give the answer. 'in the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is an air-filled hollow in the bones of the skull.
